paragraphs.text: Palagano et al. (2018) studied an Indian family with 2 affected sibs who had been diagnosed with acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis type 1. They described the disorder as an extremely rare autosomal recessive syndrome with facial and skeletal abnormalities, short stature, and intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: Palagano et al. (2018) described acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis as an autosomal recessive syndrome. In the Indian family they studied, the 2 affected sibs were homozygous for a truncating mutation in the NBAS gene, which is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: In the Indian family studied by Palagano et al. (2018), the 2 affected sibs with acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis were homozygous for a truncating mutation in the NBAS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We analyzed an Indian family with two affected siblings by exome sequencing and identified a novel homozygous truncating mutation in the Neuroblastoma-Amplified Sequence (NBAS) gene in the patients' genome.

checks.claim: Homozygosity for the NBAS truncating mutation in the 2 affected sibs of the Indian family is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance of acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis.

paragraphs.text: Palagano et al. (2018) used exome sequencing in 2 affected sibs from an Indian family with acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis and identified a novel homozygous truncating mutation in the NBAS gene. When the truncated NBAS protein was overexpressed in HEK293T cells, both nonsense-mediated decay and Golgi-to-endoplasmic reticulum retrograde traffic were impaired.

paragraphs.text: Using immunohistochemistry, Palagano et al. (2018) found that the NBAS protein was expressed in mouse embryos. Expression was seen in developing chondrogenic and osteogenic skeletal structures and in the cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum. In zebrafish embryos, depleting endogenous z-nbas caused defective morphogenesis of the chondrogenic cranial skeletal elements.
